title: Inspecting 1D & 2D Array Shapes
description: Understand how .shape, .size, and .ndim describe 1-dimensional vectors and 2-dimensional matrices.
code:
import numpy as np

# 1D Vector (One line)
vector = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print("Vector:", vector)
print("Vector shape:", vector.shape)
print("Vector dimensions (ndim):", vector.ndim)
print("Vector total size:", vector.size)

# 2D Matrix (Rows and Columns)
matrix = np.array([
    [10, 20],
    [30, 40]
])
print("\nMatrix:\n", matrix)
print("Matrix shape:", matrix.shape)
print("Matrix dimensions (ndim):", matrix.ndim)
print("Matrix total size:", matrix.size)
expectedOutput:
Vector: [10 20 30 40]
Vector shape: (4,)
Vector dimensions (ndim): 1
Vector total size: 4

Matrix:
 [[10 20]
 [30 40]]
Matrix shape: (2, 2)
Matrix dimensions (ndim): 2
Matrix total size: 4
explanation: vector.shape returns (4,) because it has one axis with 4 items. matrix.shape returns (2, 2) representing 2 rows and 2 columns. Both have size 4, but different dimensional arrangements.

title: Reshaping 1D Array to 2D Matrix
description: Transform 6 elements into a 2x3 matrix and verify that the total element count is conserved.
code:
import numpy as np

numbers = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60])
print("Original 1D array:", numbers)
print("Original shape:", numbers.shape)

# Reshape to 2 rows and 3 columns
grid = numbers.reshape(2, 3)
print("\nReshaped 2D matrix (2x3):\n", grid)
print("New shape:", grid.shape)
print("New dimensions:", grid.ndim)

# Alternative valid reshape: 3 rows and 2 columns
grid_3x2 = numbers.reshape(3, 2)
print("\nAlternative 2D matrix (3x2):\n", grid_3x2)
print("Alternative shape:", grid_3x2.shape)
expectedOutput:
Original 1D array: [10 20 30 40 50 60]
Original shape: (6,)

Reshaped 2D matrix (2x3):
 [[10 20 30]
 [40 50 60]]
New shape: (2, 3)
New dimensions: 2

Alternative 2D matrix (3x2):
 [[10 20]
 [30 40]
 [50 60]]
Alternative shape: (3, 2)
explanation: Both reshape(2, 3) and reshape(3, 2) succeed because 2*3 = 6 and 3*2 = 6. The values stay identical; only the tabular grid arrangement shifts.

title: Row Vectors vs Column Vectors
description: Compare a 1x4 row vector with a 4x1 column vector.
code:
import numpy as np

data = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])

# Reshape to a Row Vector (1 row, 4 columns)
row_vector = data.reshape(1, 4)
print("Row Vector (1, 4):\n", row_vector)
print("Row Vector shape:", row_vector.shape)

# Reshape to a Column Vector (4 rows, 1 column)
col_vector = data.reshape(4, 1)
print("\nColumn Vector (4, 1):\n", col_vector)
print("Column Vector shape:", col_vector.shape)
expectedOutput:
Row Vector (1, 4):
 [[10 20 30 40]]
Row Vector shape: (1, 4)

Column Vector (4, 1):
 [[10]
 [20]
 [30]
 [40]]
Column Vector shape: (4, 1)
explanation: A shape of (1, 4) produces a horizontal single-row matrix. A shape of (4, 1) produces a vertical 4-row column. Both are 2D arrays (ndim=2), unlike the flat 1D vector (4,).

title: Tuple Unpacking with Array Shape
description: Unpack rows and columns directly from the shape tuple and access values via coordinate indexing.
code:
import numpy as np

marks = np.array([
    80, 75, 90,
    70, 85, 88,
    92, 78, 95
])

# Reshape into a 3x3 table (3 students x 3 subjects)
gradebook = marks.reshape(3, 3)

# Tuple unpacking
num_students, num_subjects = gradebook.shape
print(f"Roster: {num_students} students x {num_subjects} subjects")
print("Gradebook:\n", gradebook)

# Coordinate indexing: gradebook[row, col]
# Student 2 (row 1), Subject 3 (col 2)
val = gradebook[1, 2]
print(f"Student 2, Subject 3 Mark: {val}")
expectedOutput:
Roster: 3 students x 3 subjects
Gradebook:
 [[80 75 90]
 [70 85 88]
 [92 78 95]]
Student 2, Subject 3 Mark: 88
explanation: gradebook.shape returns the tuple (3, 3), which can be unpacked into two variables: num_students and num_subjects. gradebook[1, 2] retrieves the element at row index 1 and column index 2.
